Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case — a simple condition that stops the calling — otherwise it would run forever. Each time the function calls itself, it moves closer to that base case, and the results get combined as the calls "unwind." A classic example is calculating factorials: factorial(5) calls factorial(4), which calls factorial(3), and so on until it hits factorial(1), then multiplies its way back up.

4. For example, factorial(5) computes 5 × factorial(4), which computes 4 × factorial(3), and so on until it reaches factorial(1) = 1, then multiplies the results back together.
